::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[What does it mean to multiply a vector by a set?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/5103094/what-does-it-mean-to-multiply-a-vector-by-a-set), asked by [Robert Cudmore](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/1704218/robert-cudmore) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2025-10-21; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> In my textbook, the following result is stated as obvious:
>
> > If $B \subset \mathbf{R}^n$ is compact and $x \in \mathbf{R}^m$, it is easy to see that $\{x\} \times B \subset \mathbf{R}^{n+m}$ is compact. However, a much stronger assertion can be made.
>
> Although I think I can understand the logic behind the proof, I'm having  difficulty visualising what $\{x\} \times B$ means. Is there an intuitive way to understand this? I can't find many resources online.
>
>   [q-picture attached]: FyNiFAVo.png
:::

For some intuition, set $n=m=1$. Let $B$ be the closed interval $[a,b]$, and $x \in \mathbb{R}$. Then $\{x\} \times B$ is the set of all $(x,y)$, where $a \leq y \leq b$. This is the closed line segment joining $(x,a)$ and $(x,b)$ in the plane.

For general $n$ and $m$, continue to think of the first $n$ coordinates as along an “$x$-axis”, and the last $m$ as along the “$y$-axis.” Then $\{x\} \times B$ translates the set $B$ over to the point where it lies over $x$. 
This is just another version of $B$, which is why the author says it's obvious that $\{x\} \times B$ is compact.
